OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $h_3(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that there exists a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with chromatic number $k$. Find an asymptotic for $h_3(k)$, and also prove\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{h_3(k+1)}{h_3(k)}=1.\]
#1013: [Er71]
graph theory | 
chromatic number
The function $h_3(k)$ is dual to the function $f(n)$ considered in [1104], in that $h_3(k)= n$ if and only if $n$ is minimal such that $f(n)=k$.
Graver and Yackel [GrYa68] proved\[h_3(k)\gg \frac{\log k}{\log\log k}k^2.\]The bounds for $f(n)$ from [1104] imply\[\left(\frac{1}{2}-o(1)\right)k^2\log k\leq h_3(k) \leq (1+o(1))k^2\log k.\]See also [920] for a generalisation to $K_r$-free graphs.
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla, Stijn Cambie, and Zach Hunter

 I think this is the other way around - if $R(3,n/k)>n$ then there is a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with independence number $\leq n/k$, and so chromatic number $\geq k$, and hence (deleting vertices if necessary to get chromatic number $=k$) $h_3(k) \leq n$. 
Johansson's bound for the chromatic number of triangle-free graphs (if I've found the right result) says that $\chi(G) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}$, which implies the lower bound $h_3(k)\gg (\log k)k$, which is weaker than the Graver-Yackel bound given here.
EDIT: In fact this is the dual function to [1104].

 For the record: as in problem 1104, the application of Johansson's theorem is more subtle. It says that $\chi(G)\ll \frac{\Delta}{ \log \Delta}$ where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of a triangle-free graph $G$. This implies $\chi(G)\ll \sqrt {\frac{n}{\log n}}$, hence $h_3(k) \gg k^2 \log k$. The proof in a nutshell: If $\Delta \leq \sqrt{n \log n}$ then it's immediate. Otherwise select a vertex $v$ with maximum degree and apply induction to $G-N[v]$.

 Johansson's result was in a technical report "Asymptotic choice number for triangle free graphs" from 1996, which he famously never published.
There doesn't seem to exist a stable link to the report online, and I have never seen it. However, if I remember well, the write-up in chapters 12 and 13 of the book "Graph colouring and the probabilistic method"(2002) by Michael Molloy and Bruce Reed follows Johansson's proof.
It used a rather technical (semi-random) method. Since 2017 there have been shorter proofs and improvements, using e.g. entropy compression, or Lovász Local Lemma, and even just the first moment method.
